The Civil Aviation Authority of New Zealand (CAA)
The CAA is a government body whose task is to set policy and standards and promulgate rules and procedures for safe and efficient operation of aircraft.
The Airways Corporation of New Zealand
A state-owned enterprise whose main task is to provide the air traffic services required by aircraft.
Meteorological Service of New Zealand Ltd
The Meteorological Service is a State-Owned Enterprise (SOE) whose function includes providing meteorological information to aviation.
ASPEQ (formerly ASL)
ASPEQ is a company owned by the NZ aviation industry whose task it is to administer many of the licensing functions such as examinations.
Airport Companies
Many airports throughout the country are administered and operated by airport companies.
International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)
ICAO is a worldwide body whose task is to set standards and practices for international civil aviation.
Airways New Zealand has established a National Briefing Office situated at the Control Centre at Christchurch which also houses the FIC and NOTAM office.
The briefing office receives all flight plans, processes them and sends them to the units requiring copies.

Registering aircraft.

CAA Rules are produced by the CAA and contain rules that are applicable to civil aviation activities in NZ.
There are two types of CA rules:
Ordinary Rules
They are evolved through a sometimes-lengthy consultative process.
Emergency Rules
These are produced by the authority (or Director) in cases where urgent action is required.
CA Rules are divided into Parts, each Part dealing with a particular aspect of civil aviation.
CAR Parts are further divided into Subparts. For example, CAR Part 91 Subpart A.
ACs are issued by the CAA.
They contain information about standards, practices and procedures promulgated in CA Rules.
Many of the CARs have associated ACs that further explain the requirements of the CAR Part.
The NZAIP is produced by the Airways Corporation in association with the CAA.
The NZAIP contains orders, technical procedures and information of a lasting nature necessary for flight operations and consists of the following parts:
Volume 1 which contains all the general written information.
Volume 2 & 3 which deal with additional written material and charts relating to IFR flights.
Volume 4 which deals with additional written material and charts relating to VFR flights.
The NZAIP Supplement which contains amendments and additions to the NZAIP documents as well as information that is of a temporary nature.

Periodically an NZAIP Bulletin is issued comprising of new pages for the NZAIP documents.
Amendments to the NZAIP are distributed at least 28 days in advance of effective date. (GEN 3.1)
NOTAMs are issued by the CAA, the Airways Corporation or the airport Operator.
They contain written material essential to flight safety that needs to be promulgated without delay.
A Type – Sent domestically
B Type – Sent internationally
NOTAMs are issued per area.

Notices containing information that doesn’t qualify as a NOTAM.
Relates to flight safety, air navigation or technical/administrative matters.

Within most documents the word ‘shall’ or ‘must’ means the instruction or rule must be complied with.
The word ‘should’ means that a recommendation is being made.
The NZAIP Vol 1 GEN 2.2, and CAR Part 1 list most of the commonly used abbreviations.

Co-ordinated Universal Time (UTC) is used for all flights within NZ, the day beginning at 0000 hours and ending at 2400 hours.
NZ Standard Time (NZST) is 12 hours ahead of UTC and NZ Daylight Time (NZDT) is 13 hours ahead of UTC.
NZ Daylight Time (NZDT ) commences at 0200 NZST on the last Sunday in September and ceases at 0300 NZDT on the first Sunday in April.
Date and Time is expressed as a six-figure group comprising the day, hours and minutes.
For example, the 8th of May 6:45pm is expressed as 081845 UTC
For NOTAMs and preflight information, a ten-figure group comprising the year, month, day, hours and minutes is used.
For example, the 28th of September 2002 1845NZST is expressed as 0209280645 UTC

Appropriate:
In respect of a licence or rating, this means applicable to the same aircraft category.
Category:
In respect of an aircraft, this means the classification of an aircraft as an aeroplane, balloon, glider, hang glider, helicopter, microlight or parachute.
Co-pilot:
A licenced pilot, serving in any piloting capacity other than Pilot-in-Command, but does not include a pilot receiving flight instruction from a pilot onboard the aircraft.
Cross-country flight:
A flight that extends more than 25 nautical miles in a straight-line distance from the middle of the aerodrome of departure.
Day:

The hours between the beginning of morning civil twilight, which is when the centre of the rising sun’s disc is 6 degrees below the horizon; and the end of evening civil twilight, which is when the centre of the setting sun’s disc is 6 degrees below the horizon:
Dual flight time:
A flight during which a person is receiving flight instruction from an appropriately licenced and rated pilot on board a dual control aircraft.
Flight crew member:
Any person assigned by an Operator for duty as a member of the crew of the aircraft.
This shows that a student undergoing dual instruction is not a passenger but a flight crew member.
Flight Examiner:
A person approved by the Director or authorised under the rules to conduct specified flight tests or ZFT simulator tests for flight crew licences or ratings.
Flight Time:

Or an aircraft other than a balloon, the total time from the moment an aircraft first moves for the purpose of flight until the moment it comes to rest at the end of the flight including any associated push back, taxiing and subsequent holding time;
For a balloon, the total time from burner on for the purpose of inflation for flight until the envelope is completely deflated at the end of a flight.
Night:
The hours between the end of Evening Civil Twilight and the beginning of Morning Civil Twilight.
Operate:

In relation to an aircraft, this means to fly or use the aircraft, or to cause or permit the aircraft to fly, be used, or be in any place, whether or not the person is present with the aircraft; ‘Operator’ has a corresponding meaning.
Pilot-in-Command:
In relation to any aircraft, this means the pilot responsible for operation and safety of the aircraft.
Rating:
An authorisation entered on a licence, certificate, or logbook, specifying additional privileges.
Each pilot of an aircraft must hold an appropriate current pilot licence (except students).
Pilot licences currently available are:
Private Pilot Licence (PPL)
Commercial Pilot Licence (CPL)
Airline Transport Pilot Licence (ATPL)
Pilot licences are issued for the lifetime of the holder. Where necessary the Director may revoke or issue a temporary licence or rating.
NOTE:

A conviction for any offence relating to alcohol or drugs, or a refusal to submit to any test for alcohol or drugs, shall be relevant for determining whether a person is, or remains, a fit and proper person to hold a licence or rating.
Such a conviction may result in a refusal to grant a licence/rating or to suspend or revoke it.
The ratings available are:
Flight Radiotelephone Operator Rating.
Aircraft Type Ratings.
Aerobatic Rating.
Basic Gas Turbine Rating.
Instrument Rating.
Flight Instructor Ratings – E,D,C,B, and A.
Airline, General Aviation, and Transitional Flight Examiner Rating
Glider Tow Rating
Parachute Drop Rating
Pilot Chemical Rating
Agricultural Rating – Grade 2 and 1
First Aid Rating
An applicant for a written exam shall produce written proof (photo ID) of his or her identity.
The pass mark in all exams is 70%.
Amendment to Part 61.17 and 61.18 now places restrictions on the validity of exam credits.
Cheating in any exam may result in:
Failure in that subject
Disqualification of all or any subjects already passed.
Debarment from sitting other exams for up to 12 months.
Suspension or revocation of any licence or rating.
Every pilot shall maintain a record in ink of their flight time and instrument time in an approved pilot logbook.
Flight time entered in a pilot’s logbook that has been lost or destroyed shall only be accepted by the Director for crediting purposes if it can be substantiated by means acceptable to the Director.
Entries in pilot logbooks shall be made within the following periods after the completion of the flight to be recorded:
for Operations not for hire or reward, flight training, domestic air operations, and special operations - 7 days.
for International Air Transport Operations and aerial work operations (other than flight training operations) - 14 days.
However, if a pilot is engaged in flying away from base where the logbook would normally be expected to be kept, the specified periods may be extended to 48 hours after return to base.
Every pilot shall keep his or her pilot logbook for at least 12 months from the date of the last flight time entry recorded in it.
Before a pilot submits his or her pilot logbook to the Director for any required inspection, the pilot shall:
on each page, total each column of entries.
in the spaces provided, enter his or her total flight experience.
below the last entry, certify the correctness of the entries.
sign the certification.
Flight time during which:
a pilot is receiving dual instruction shall be logged as dual flight time and shall include a record of the air exercises undertaken.
a pilot is receiving command practice under the supervision of a Pilot-in-Command designated by the Operator to give command supervision shall be logged as command practice.
a pilot is gaining instrument flight experience under actual or simulated instrument flight conditions shall be logged as instrument flight time.
General
Any person, whether or not the holder of a current licence, may fly dual with a Flight Instructor and log those hours as dual flight time.
Solo flight requirements
A person who does not hold a current Pilot Licence shall not fly solo unless:
That person is at least 16 years of age.
That person holds at least a current Class 2 medical.
That person has sufficient ability in reading, speaking and understanding English.
The flight is carried out under the supervision of a Category C, B or A Flight Instructor, except that first solos must be authorised by a Cat A or B.
Solo flight requirements
The holder of a Category B or A Flight Instructor rating has certified in that person's logbook that he or she has received instruction in and demonstrated competency in the required exercises.
That person has received dual instruction within the last 5 hours of flight experience unless otherwise authorised by the holder of a Category B or A Flight Instructor rating.
That person has had piloting experience in appropriate aircraft within the immediately preceding 30 days.
For solo cross-country flight, the flight is authorised by an A or B Category Flight Instructor and the student holds all PPL written exam credits.
Limitations
A person who does not hold a current pilot licence shall not act as a Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft:
For remuneration.
If the aircraft is being operated for hire or reward.
If any other person is being carried other than a Flight Examiner.
For overseas flights.
Eligibility Requirements
To be eligible for a private pilot licence a person shall:
Be at least 17 years old.
Hold at least a Class 2 medical certificate.
50 hours of flight time as a pilot in appropriate aircraft comprising solo flight time, dual flight time, instrument time and cross-country flight time acceptable to the Director.

If the person is not seeking to exercise private pilot privileges on cross-countries, 40 hours of flight time as a pilot in appropriate aircraft comprising solo flight time, dual flight time, instrument time and cross-country flight time acceptable to the Director.
If the person seeks to exercise private pilot privileges by night, have night flight experience acceptable to the Director.
Have passed approved written examinations relevant to the VFR operation of light aircraft in New Zealand in:
- Air law.
- Air Navigation and Flight Planning.
- Meteorology.
- Aircraft Technical Knowledge.
- Human Factors.
- Flight Radiotelephony.

Demonstrate to a Flight Examiner general knowledge of and ability to perform competently, those normal and emergency flight manoeuvres applicable to the type of aircraft in which the applicant is being flight tested, and ability to comply with air traffic practices and procedures.
Privileges and limitations:
A current Private Pilot Licence authorises the
holder to:

act, but not for remuneration, as Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft for which the licence is granted, and for which the pilot holds a type rating, and that is not operated for hire or reward, and to carry passengers in that aircraft; and

act, but not for remuneration, as co-pilot of an aircraft of the category for which the licence is granted, and for which the pilot holds a type rating, and that is not operated for hire or reward, and which is required to be operated with a co-pilot.
The holder of a Private Pilot Licence shall not act as Pilot-in-Command or as co-pilot of an aircraft:
at night.
on a cross-country flight.
unless an appropriately qualified Flight Instructor has certified in that holder's logbook that the holder has satisfactorily completed the flight training required to perform that activity.
The holder of a current private pilot licence may act, but not for remuneration, as Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft that is operated for hire or reward in order to:
tow a glider in flight, provided the operation is under the direct control of the holder of an aviation recreation organisation certificate.
carry persons intending to make a parachute descent, provided the operation is under the direct control of the holder of an aviation recreation organisation certificate.
Currency requirements
In order to keep a PPL current, the holder must:
Continue to meet the required medical standard.
To carry passengers, meet recent flight experience requirements.
3 take-off and landings as P.I.C
1 take off and landing with an A or B Cat instructor
Recent flight test
Have completed a Biennial Flight Review within the last 2 years.
AC 61 prescribes the requirements for aircraft type ratings.
The following is a summary of the eligibility requirements:
Dual conversion flight experience acceptable to the Director.
For turbine powered aircraft a Basic Gas Turbine Rating must be held.
Demonstrate satisfactory technical knowledge of the aircraft and in the case of aircraft over 5700kg, have passed a written exam.
Demonstrate competency to fly the aircraft.
When the rating is issued, the “Rating Certificate" in the pilot's logbook is endorsed and signed by the issuing Instructor.

An aircraft type rating allows you to exercise your licence privileges in all aircraft of the same type which is defined in CAR Part 1 as “all aircraft of the same basic design, including all modifications thereto except those modifications which result in a significant change in handling or flight characteristics.”
Requirements
Have satisfactorily completed an aerobatics ground course at an organisation holding an approved certificate for the purpose.
Have satisfactorily completed an aerobatics flight training course at an organisation holding an approved certificate for the purpose.
Has demonstrated competency to an authorised person to conduct the assessment.
Issue

When the Approved Training Organisation is satisfied the requirements for the issue of an aerobatic flight rating have been met, the rating shall be issued by entering the appropriate endorsement in the person’s logbook.
Upon application, the endorsement can also be entered on the persons pilot’s licence.
Privileges and Limitations
A holder of an aerobatic rating can conduct aerobatic manoeuvres:
At least 3000ft above the surface while carrying passengers.
At least 1500ft above the surface while not carrying passengers.
Below 1500ft above the surface, while not carrying passengers, at an aviation event, and when authorised by the holder of an Aviation Training Organisation certificate.
Currency requirements

A holder of an aerobatic rating shall not exercise the privileges of the rating unless within the last 2 years (or within 60 days prior to the due date) they have demonstrated continued competency to an approved person.
3000ft AGL
1500ft AGL
Ground

The holder of a licence or rating shall, when required by the Director and within such period as the Director may determine, take an examination or test to demonstrate his or her proficiency in the capacity for which the licence or rating is held.
Any examination or test required by the Director shall consist of such part or parts of the examination or test required by this Part as the Director may determine.

A person who takes an examination or test and who fails to comply with the requirements prescribed for the grant of the licence or rating held, shall not exercise the privileges of that licence or rating.
Air operations are those involving the carriage of persons or goods by air for hire and reward.
Operators must hold appropriate certificates and pilots must hold at least a current Commercial Pilot’s Licence.
Costs may be shared between a licenced pilot and passengers for flights carrying passengers only, which:
Are not advertised to the public.
The pilot receives no payment or other reward for their services.
The costs of the flight are shared between pilot and passengers equally.
No other charges or rewards, other than the costs of the flight, shall be paid by any person on the flight.
Private Pilot – Day Flight
The holder of a Private Pilot Licence shall not act as Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft carrying passengers by day, unless:
within the immediately preceding 90 days, that person has carried out as Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft of the same type, or of a ZFT simulator, not less than 3 takeoffs and 3 landings by day; or
that person has satisfactorily demonstrated, to a Flight Examiner, continued proficiency by day in an aircraft of the same type.
Private pilot – Night Flight
The holder of a Private Pilot Licence shall not act as Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft carrying passengers at night, unless:
within the immediately preceding 90 days, that person has carried out as Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft of the same type, or of a ZFT simulator, not less than 3 take-offs and 3 landings by night; or
that person has satisfactorily demonstrated, to a Flight Examiner, continued proficiency by night in an aircraft of the same type; or
at least 1 take-off and landing with a Cat A or B instructor
- except that if compliance with day recency can be shown, the experience by night need not be in an aircraft of the same type.

The holder of a pilot’s licence shall not exercise the privileges of that licence for longer than 2 years from the date of the issue or renewal flight test for that licence unless the holder has successfully completed a flight review within the immediately preceding 2 years.
A record to that effect must be endorsed in the holder's logbook.
A Biennial Flight Review shall be conducted by an appropriately qualified Flight Instructor and shall consist of:

A review of the current general operating and flight rules applicable to the use of the licence under review, with particular emphasis upon applicable changes introduced within the immediately preceding 2-year period.
Flight instruction to review those manoeuvres and procedures applicable to the use of the licence under review.
Some pilots are exempt from this requirement when conducting air operations as they complete yearly competency checks.
When a Flight Instructor is satisfied that a flight review has been successfully completed, the Flight Instructor shall certify the pilot’s logbook to that effect.

lessons.title: Use of lower licence or rating

content.content: The holder of a licence who does not meet the currency requirements, but who meets those requirements for a lower licence, may exercise the privileges of that lower licence.
For example, if you are the holder of a CPL licence but your Class 1 medical has expired, you can exercise the privileges of your PPL on Class 2 medical.

Where the privileges of a licence issued under Part 61 have not been exercised for 5 years or more, the licence holder shall pass an approved Air Law examination and pass an appropriate issue flight test before the privileges of that licence may be exercised again.
The law requires that pilots attain and maintain certain medical standards.
CAR Part 67 details these medical standards.
Medical assessments are conducted by a Designated Medical Examiner (DME) or Aviation Medical Assessor (AMA)
The three classes of medical certificates are:
Class 1
Class 2
Class 3
Issued for a period no longer than:
6 months where the applicant is age 40 or more, and is engaged in single crew air transport operations carrying passengers.
12 months in all other cases.
On the date that the medical certificate was issued.
Issued for a period no longer than:
60 months where the applicant is less than age 40
24 months where the applicant is age 40 or more
Issued for a period no longer than:
48 months where the applicant is less than age 40
24 months where the applicant is age 40 or older.

A person holding a pilot licence shall not exercise the privileges of that licence and students acting as Pilot-in-Command shall not fly solo unless that person holds an appropriate current medical certificate.
Any medical deficiency or medical question must be referred to your aviation medical specialist.
State the normal currency period of the Land Transport medical certificate (DL9) for a holder who is under the age of 40 as per Rule 61
Was issued within the previous 5 years
State the normal currency period of the Land Transport medical certificate (DL9) for a holder who is 40 years of age or more on the date that the certificate is issued as per Rule 61
Was issued in the previous 24 Months
Aircraft
Can derive support in the atmosphere from the reactions of air, otherwise than by the reactions of the air against the surface of the Earth.
Aeroplane
A power-driven, heavier-than-air aircraft deriving its lift in flight chiefly from aerodynamic reactions on surfaces which remain fixed under given conditions of flight.
Aircraft Category
Any one of the following classes of aircraft- aeroplane, helicopter, glider, balloon.
Aircraft Component
Any component part of an aircraft up to and including a complete airframe or power plant, and includes any operational or emergency equipment fitted to, or provided in an aircraft.
Approved
Unless used in reference to another person, this means approved in writing by the Director.
Flight Manual

An approved manual, associated with the certificate of airworthiness, containing limitations within which the aircraft may be considered airworthy, and instructions and information necessary to the flight crew members for the safe operation of the aircraft.
Helicopter
A heavier-than-air aircraft supported in flight chiefly by the reactions of air on one or more power driven rotors on a substantially vertical axis.
Glider
A non-power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft which derives its lift in flight chiefly from aerodynamic reactions on surfaces which remain fixed under given conditions of flight.
Maintenance
In relation to an aircraft or aircraft component, this means all work and inspections performed to ensure the continued airworthiness of the aircraft or aircraft component and all modifications.
Microlight Aircraft
A basic low performance aircraft designed to carry not more than two persons which meets low momentum parameters that are acceptable to the Director.
Operate

In relation to an aircraft, this means to fly or use the aircraft, or to cause or permit the aircraft to fly, be used, or be in any place, whether or not the person is present with the aircraft; and “Operator” has a corresponding meaning.
Owner
In relation to an aircraft, this includes any person lawfully entitled to the possession of the aircraft for 28 days or longer.
No person may operate an aircraft unless the following documents are carried in the aircraft:
the current Airworthiness Certificate or a certified copy of the current Airworthiness Certificate.
the Aircraft Flight Manual.

for New Zealand registered aircraft, the Technical Log required, unless for aircraft operating under an Air Operator Certificate from a fixed base, an alternative means acceptable to the Director issued to inform the pilot of the maintenance status of the aircraft.
CAA Form 2173 Weight and balance
CAA Form 2129 Radio station equipment approval levels
Note: NZ registered aircraft flying overseas, and foreign aircraft flying in NZ shall carry the aircraft’s certificate of registration.
When an aircraft is entered onto the NZ Register of Aircraft, a Certificate of Registration is issued in the name of the owner.
If the aircraft is hired or leased to anyone for more than 28 days, the Certificate of Registration must be re-issued to the person or organisation hiring or leasing.
The Certificate of Registration expires the moment the person lawfully entitled to possession of the aircraft ceases to have such possession.
An aircraft may then be operated without a Certificate of Registration for 28 days by another person who is lawfully entitled to possession of the aircraft.
The Airworthiness Certificate is a document issued for an aircraft when the Director is satisfied that the aircraft is in an airworthy condition.
This certificate is specific to an individual aircraft.
There are three categories:
Standard – AC21-2 – Eligible for the carriage of persons or goods for hire or reward operations under Part 91 and eligible for air transport operations under Part 119.
Restricted – AC21-2 - Eligible for the carriage of persons or goods for hire or reward operations under Part 91

Special AC21-3 - A special category airworthiness certificate can be issued to an aircraft, that cannot meet the criteria for the issue of an airworthiness certificate in the standard category or restricted category. E.g built aircraft, light sport aircraft
No person may operate an aircraft unless:
it has a current Airworthiness Certificate.
it is in an airworthy condition.
A person operating an aircraft issued with an Airworthiness Certificate must comply with:
any operating limitations issued with the Airworthiness Certificate.
the markings and placards that are required by the Civil Aviation Rules to be displayed in the aircraft.

A person may operate an aircraft without a current Airworthiness Certificate for the purpose of demonstrating the eligibility of the aircraft for the issue, renewal, or reinstatement of an Airworthiness Certificate if:
a type certificate or type acceptance certificate for the aircraft type is in force.
the aircraft complies with the requirements in Part 21.191 (certification of components and parts).
a suitably qualified person certifies that the aircraft is fit for flight.
the Pilot-in-Command is the holder of an appropriate, current pilot licence and type rating.
no other person is carried unless that person performs an essential function in connection with the operation.
This category allows most aircraft operations under various CA rules.
This category generally applies to aircraft used in the agricultural role when certain load limitations may be exceeded.
Restricted category Airworthiness Certificate -
operating limitations.
No person shall operate an aircraft issued with a Restricted Category Airworthiness Certificate under flight instruction other than:
Conversion instruction for a Type Rating.
Flight Instruction for the issue of an Agricultural Rating.
Flight Instruction for the specific operational purpose for which the aircraft is certificated.
This category applies to aircraft that do not comply with Standard or Restricted Category requirements.
It is further divided into:
Experimental Certificate
Applies to aircraft such as amateur-built aircraft and ‘Warbirds’ type aircraft.
Special Flight Permit
This is issued to allow a specific flight or series of flights for flight test or other specific circumstances.
A flight test after maintenance does not require a special flight permit. They are categorised as Operational Flight Checks.
Special Category Airworthiness Certificates –Operating limitations.
No person may operate an aircraft that has a Special Category Airworthiness Certificate for the carriage of persons or goods for hire or reward.
This does not apply to a person operating an aircraft for the carriage of persons for hire or reward where the person being carried is:
the holder of a Flight Instructor Rating.
giving conversion instruction to the Operator.

Except in the case of takeoff and landing, no person may operate an aircraft that has a Special Category Airworthiness Certificate over a congested area of a city or town unless the aircraft has been authorised to do so by the Director in writing.
A person operating an aircraft that has a Special Category Airworthiness Certificate must advise each person carried in the aircraft of the category of Airworthiness Certificate held.
Some aircraft can be issued an Airworthiness Certificate in more than one category if it can be readily changed from one configuration to another.
A Standard and Restricted Category may be issued to helicopters which operate on Agricultural Operations as well as carrying passengers.
If the aircraft is sold the certificate remains with the aircraft.
The Technical Log is an approved document which provides details to the pilot of the maintenance status of the aircraft.
Items to be entered into the Tech Log by the Operator are:
Name of the Operator, aircraft registration, type and model.
The maintenance program under which the aircraft is maintained.
Status of maintenance including date and identity of the next scheduled inspection.
Date or hours at which other maintenance is due prior to the next scheduled inspection.
Date at which next annual Review of Airworthiness or Maintenance Review is due.
Daily hours flown and total time in service.
Daily cycles used or total cycles, if applicable.
Any defects found by a pilot during or following a flight.
Rectification of defects.
Details of any deferred rectifications including inoperative equipment with which the aircraft may be flown.
Signature of the Maintenance Engineer certifying that the appropriate maintenance, rectification or deferral has been carried out in accordance with the rules.
The Flight Manual is generally written and produced by the constructor of the aircraft.
It contains operational information about the aircraft as well as recommended handling techniques.
No person shall operate an aircraft unless it is operated in compliance with the operating limitations specified in the aircraft Flight Manual.
Each holder of a NZ certificate of registration shall ensure that the aircraft bears registration markings and in the case of aircraft over 5700kg nationality markings.
The first letter of the registration marking may be omitted by an aircraft operating in NZ if they are:
Helicopters when the registration starts with an ‘H’.
Gliders, powered gliders and balloons.
Would usually be HQE
When an aircraft is registered in New Zealand it is issued a registration consisting of ZK- followed by three letters, e.g.,
ZK-NFO.
There are three types of aircraft callsigns in use in New Zealand:
Type C
Type B
Type A
Type C callsigns consist of the aircraft type plus the last three letters of its registration.
Cessna 152 November Foxtrot Oscar
The type of aircraft is given so that the controller knows the operational performance of the aircraft.
Once the aircraft has been addressed by the ground station it is permissible to use only the last three letters of the registration.
Type B callsigns consist of the telephony designator of the aircraft operating agency, plus the last three letters of the registration.
Mainland Kilo Victor Whiskey
Once again once contact is established the last three letters suffice.
Type A callsigns consist of the aircraft operating agencies Telephony Designator followed by the Flight Identification.
Chatham's Seven Zero Zero
Unlike Type B & C, Type A cannot be abbreviated, and must always be used in full.
When an aircraft has been designed, built, tested and approved, it is issued a Type Certificate in the country of origin.
An aircraft with a foreign Type Certificate may be granted a NZ Type Acceptance Certificate which means that the NZ authorities have accepted the foreign certification of the aircraft.
https://www.caa.govt.nz/aircraft/type-acceptance-reps/#Aeroplanes
The Operator of an aircraft shall ensure that:
The aircraft is maintained in an airworthy condition.
Applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) are complied with.
The aircraft is inspected in conformity with Part 91, the Operator’s Maintenance Manual or in conformity with another approved maintenance program.

An annual or 100-hour inspection has been carried out in the last 12 months or the preceding 100 hours time in service (which ever comes first) unless the aircraft is maintained under an approved maintenance schedule which does not require an annual or 100-hour inspection.
Mandatory replacement times published in airworthiness limitations of a manufacturer’s manual have been carried out.
Radios, altimeter system, transponder(s) and ELT(s) have been maintained, tested and inspected at regular intervals in accordance with requirements laid down in Part 91.
An Annual Review of Airworthiness (ARA) or a Maintenance Review has been carried out by a suitably qualified person within the preceding 12 months.
All maintenance is carried out in accordance with CAR Parts 91 and 43.

A person who holds a pilot’s licence with an appropriate type rating may perform certain maintenance tasks provided the pilot is authorised by the Operator and by the maintenance provider’s Chief Engineer.
List of Pilot Maintenance:
Replacement of tyres or tail skids.
Greasing and lubrication involving no disassembly other than the removal of access panels.
Simple fabric patch repairs which do not involve removal of aircraft controls or repairs of control surfaces
Restoration of decorative coatings provided no disassembly or disturbance of any operating systems, or control surface restoration, are involved.
Simple repairs to fairings or non-structural plates.
Replacing of side windows not affecting structure or any operating system.
Replacing the aircraft battery.
Replacing fuses or lights.
Simple installation of GPS receivers.
Replenishment of hydraulic fluid in hydraulic reservoirs.
Compressor washing (with restrictions).
Installation and removal of role equipment.
A release to service normally takes the form of an entry in the appropriate aircraft logbook.
Note: the full release to service does not appear on the technical log.

When required servicing or maintenance has been satisfactorily completed, the licenced aircraft engineer certifies in the tech log and logbook that the work has been carried out in accordance with current NZ CAA Rules.

An aircraft which has undergone maintenance shall not be flown unless it has been certified for release to service by an authorised person and the appropriate maintenance record entries have been made.
In cases where maintenance may have affected the aircraft’s flight characteristics, an operational flight check shall be carried out by:
A pilot who is a holder of a valid pilot licence and rated on the aircraft.
No passengers (other than essential crew) are carried.
Under Part 91 no person shall operate an aircraft unless it has a current Airworthiness Certificate and is in airworthy condition.
A person may flight test an aircraft provided:
The aircraft complies with Part 21.191(b) (certification of components and parts).
A qualified person certifies the aircraft is fit to fly.
The PIC is the holder of a valid licence and rating.
No persons other than essential crew are carried.
No person shall operate an aircraft unless the static pressure system and altimeter has been tested:
Within the preceding 24 calendar months.
After any maintenance on the system.
Aircraft transponders are required in order to fly through controlled airspace which is designated ‘Transponder Mandatory’.
Aircraft which are required to have a transponder installed shall not be flown unless the transponder has been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 months.
No person shall operate an aircraft unless the ELT has:
Been tested and inspected, within the preceding 12 calendar months.
Had its batteries replaced or charged.
When the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour.
When their useful life, as determined by the manufacturer, has expired.
Under no circumstances must the ELT be tested in flight.
While testing the ELT on the ground, the following conditions apply:
Tests must be carried out in shielded areas under controlled conditions.
Do not test longer than 3 audio sweeps.
Restrict tests to the first five minutes past the hour.
Part 91.509
Minimum equipment for powered aircraft with an Airworthiness Certificate shall provide a means of indicating: Airspeed.
Altitude.
Direction.
Time.
Fuel contents (units clearly marked).
Engine RPM for each engine.
Oil Pressure for each engine.
Oil Temperature for each engine rated at over 250 horsepower using a pressure system.
Coolant Temperature for each liquid cooled engine.
Manifold Pressure for each supercharged, turbocharged or constant speed propeller equipped engine.
Cylinder Head Temperature for each air-cooled engine rated at over 250 horsepower.
Flap position, unless flap position can be determined visually by the flight crew.
Undercarriage position, if the aircraft is fitted with a retractable undercarriage.
Power generation to ascertain function of electrical power generation equipment.
For aircraft 5700kg or less and for aircraft with finite life components fitted, an aircraft flying time recorder which automatically records and accumulates time from takeoff to landing.
In addition to the requirements previously mentioned for day VFR, the following items are required for aircraft engaged in night VFR operations:
One Turn and Slip or Turn Co-Ordinator, or an Artificial Horizon usable through 360° in pitch and roll.
Position lights
Anti-collision lights system.
Illumination for each required instrument or indicator.
VFR aircraft operating in Controlled Airspace shall be equipped with approved two-way communication equipment (radio) which is capable of continuous communication with the appropriate ATC unit.
This rule may be waived if the pilot of an aircraft is authorised by ATC to operate VFR without radio communication equipment.

VFR aircraft operating over water at a distance more than 30 minutes flying time from shore shall be equipped with a radio capable of maintaining continuous two-way communication with the appropriate ATS unit.
For aircraft operating outside Controlled Airspace, approved radio equipment shall be installed if communication with any ATS is intended or required.
Tested and inspected every 24 months.

content.content: Aircraft operating over water, at a distance that is more than 30 minutes flying time from the nearest shore, shall be equipped with:
Approved radio communication equipment capable of providing continuous two-way communications with an appropriate ATS unit or other aeronautical facility.
Navigation equipment that can navigate the aircraft in accordance with the flight plan.
An aircraft operated over water shall be equipped with:
One life jacket for each person on board in a single engine aircraft or multi that cannot maintain 1000ft AMSL on one engine, when flying more than gliding distance from shore.
One life jacket for each person in a Multi-Engined Aircraft for flights more than 50nm from shore.
In Single Engine aircraft more than 100nm from shore, or a Multi-Engine more than 200nm from shore:
Sufficient life rafts with buoyancy and rated capacity to accommodate the occupants of the aircraft.
A survival locator light on each life raft.
A survival kit appropriately equipped for the route, attached to each life raft.
At least one pyrotechnic signalling device on each life raft.
One ELT or EPIRB.
All safety equipment must be installed in conspicuously identified locations and must be easily accessible in the event of a ditching.

An automatic ELT shall be carried on all aircraft except:
Microlight aircraft and manned free balloons.
Any aircraft equipped with not more than 1 seat, or a glider, if a portable ELT is carried (by a person).
Any glider, or powered aircraft with not more than 2 seats, when operated within 10nm from the aerodrome where it took off.
An aircraft may be operated without an automatic ELT for a period of 7 days if a portable ELT is on board and accessible to each occupant.
NOTE: ELT(s) means Emergency Locator Transmitter (survival) and EPIRB means Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon.
An aircraft may be ferried to a place to have an ELT fitted, or from a place where repairs cannot be made to a place where they can, provided no passengers are carried.
Each fuel contents gauge calibrated in US gallons shall be clearly marked as such.
A placard shall be placed in the immediate vicinity of any fuel and oil filler indicating the specification and/or grade of fuel or oil as appropriate.
Each aircraft dependent on the operation, must meet the following minimum requirements:
Instruments and equipment shall be in an operable condition, installed as per the manufacturer’s instructions and be able to be seen and operated from the pilot’s seated position.
Aircraft under 5700kg which do not have a Minimum Equipment List (MEL) may operate with inoperative instruments or equipment that are not:
Part of the VFR day certification instruments and equipment prescribed in the aircraft Type Certification.
Required for specific operations.
Required by an Airworthiness Directive.
Part 91 stipulates that no person shall operate an aircraft without at least the number of crew required by the aircraft Flight Manual.
Part 91.115 details the requirements for flight attendants to be carried. In general, they are not required on aircraft carrying 19 passengers or less.
No person shall operate an aircraft in simulated instrument flight in VMC unless:
The aircraft has two pilot stations, and one is occupied by a safety pilot who shall be the holder of a current pilot licence.
Fully functioning dual controls are installed unless otherwise approved.
The safety pilot has adequate vision forward and to each side and, if this cannot be assured, a competent observer shall supplement the vision of the safety pilot.
An acceptable means of simulating instrument flight is used by the pilot gaining instrument flight experience.
CAR part 91 requires that the PIC shall be satisfied that the aircraft is in a condition for safe flight.
During the flight the PIC must ensure safe operation of the aircraft and the safety of its occupants.
On completion of the flight the PIC shall record any defect(s) experienced during or following the flight in the Aircraft Tech log or other approved document.
Before operating the aircraft, be satisfied that the aircraft is airworthy and in a condition for safe flight, after—
(i) the documents required under 91.111 have been inspected; and
(ii) the aircraft has been inspected.

Each Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft shall give any commands necessary for the safety of the aircraft and of persons and property carried on the aircraft, including disembarking or refusing the carriage of:
any person who appears to be under the influence of alcohol or any drug where, in the opinion of the Pilot-in-Command, their carriage is likely to endanger the aircraft or its occupants.
any person, or any part of the cargo, which, in the opinion of the Pilot-in-Command, is likely to endanger the aircraft or its occupants.
The Civil Aviation Act states that the Pilot-in-Command:
Is responsible for the safe operation of the aircraft, the safety and well-being of all passengers and crew and the safety of the cargo.
Has the final authority to control the aircraft whilst in command and for the maintenance of discipline by all persons on board.

Is responsible for compliance with all relevant requirements and rules except in an emergency when, in the interest of safety, immediate action in breach of requirements, regulations and rules is necessary.
If deviation from the rule is required in an emergency, the PIC shall immediately notify ATC, and as soon as practicable notify the Director.

The Act states that a breach of any Act, requirements or rules in emergency situations in flight is only permitted if the emergency involves a danger to life or property and that the extent of the breach goes only as far as necessary and there is no other reasonable means to deal with the emergency.

The Act also states that where an emergency, not being an emergency that arises in flight, requires the urgent transportation of persons and medical or other supplies for the protection of life or property, the provision and rules may be breached provided:
The extent of the breach goes only as far as necessary.
There is no other reasonable means of dealing with the emergency.
The degree of danger in deviating from the rules is clearly less than the degree of risk in the emergency action.
The aircraft used is registered in New Zealand.
The emergency flight does not breach any airworthiness requirement.
The operation of the aircraft is conducted by a person lawfully entitled to operate the aircraft.
The aircraft Operator shall nominate the PIC.
Part 91 requires that when the flight crew of an aircraft includes more than one pilot, the Operator shall designate one of these pilots as the PIC for each period of flight.
A directional shoulder belt for:
Each flight crew seat in a helicopter.
Each flight crew seat in a training aircraft.
Each flight crew seat when operating at low level.
A shoulder harness for:
- each seat in aerobatic aircraft.
- each crew seat in aircraft with seating capacity of 10 or more passengers.
A seat and safety belt, or a berth for each person on board.

(Restraining belts are not required for persons engaged in parachute operations, and a seat is not required for infants less than 4 years of age when they are held by a safety belt attached to an adult occupying a seat).
Each passenger shall occupy a seat or berth and fasten their safety belt:
During each takeoff and landing.
When the aircraft is flying below 1000ft AGL.
When instructed to do so by the PIC.
During aerobatic flight.
At all times in an open cockpit aircraft.
Oxygen shall be installed and used in aircraft operating above 13000ft AMSL, or when flying between 10000ft and 13000ft for longer than 30 minutes.
Non-Pressurised
Each aircraft with a non-pressurised cabin that is operated at altitudes between 10000 and 13000ft AMSL for more than 30 minutes shall be equipped with:
Supplemental oxygen for continuous use by all crew members and 10% of passengers.
Therapeutic oxygen for continuous use by not less than 3% of the passengers.
At altitudes above 13000ft AMSL up to and including 25000ft AMSL:
Supplemental oxygen for continuous use by all crew members and passengers.
Therapeutic oxygen for continuous use by not less than 1% of the passengers.
Portable O2, 120 litres or sufficient quantity for continuous use by the crew for that time the cabin pressure altitude will exceed 10000ft.
Must be given by the pilot-in-command, a member of the crew, a person nominated by the operator, or by a recorded presentation.
A passenger brief is not required if the pilot-in-command determines that all the passengers are familiar with the contents of the briefing.
Passengers when on board an aircraft, when notified by a crew member, placards or signs shall:
Not smoke in any part of the aircraft
Location and operation of emergency exits
Procedures incase of an emergency
Occupy a seat and have a safety belt fastened
Use of electronic devices
Comply with any commands given by the PIC.
Part 91 stipulates that no person shall operate an aircraft unless it is operated in compliance with the operating limitations specified in the aircraft Flight Manual.

It also states that no person shall operate an aircraft unless it is registered and identified as registered as required by Part 47, or as required by the appropriate authority of a contracting State.
Before beginning a flight, the PIC is to be familiar with:
The Aircraft Flight Manual.
Operating Limitations detailed on placards, listings and/or instrument markings.
Emergency procedures and equipment.
Before commencing a flight, the PIC must obtain and become familiar with all information concerning that flight including:
The current Meteorological information.
The fuel requirements.
The alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed.
Any known or likely traffic delays that have been notified by ATS.
The status of the communication and navigation facilities to be used.
The current conditions of the aerodrome and runway lengths of runways at aerodromes of intended use.
Any takeoff and landing distance data contained in the Aircraft Flight Manual.
In the case of an aircraft powered by two or more engines:
Engine inoperative procedures.
One engine inoperative performance data.
Appropriate aeronautical chart(s) for each crew member. NZAIP VOL 4 & VNC/VPC.
Checklists in aircraft in excess of 5700kg or seating capacity of 10 or more passengers.
Passenger information signs for aircraft with 10 or more seats when the pilot's compartment is separate from the passenger compartment.
Reference Part 91.127
The place to be used by aircraft must be suitable for landing and takeoff in that aircraft.
Pilots must comply with any limitations on the use of the aerodrome as notified by the Operator.
The runway must be clear of all persons, animals, vehicles or other obstructions during takeoff and landing.
A runway cannot be used at night unless it is equipped with serviceable lighting.
When manoeuvring in the circuit, the aircraft must not conflict with any other nearby aerodrome circuit or instrument approach traffic
Parts of the manoeuvring area that have been notified or marked as being unsafe shall not be used. Generally, these areas are marked by white crosses, cones and/or marker boards.
When flying in the vicinity of an aerodrome, pilots are to observe other traffic so that collisions are avoided and:
Unless otherwise authorised or instructed by ATC, conform with or avoid the aerodrome traffic circuit formed by other traffic.
Except for agricultural aircraft operations, perform a left-hand circuit when approaching for landing or after takeoff unless:
Otherwise authorised by ATC.
A right-hand circuit has been prescribed.
A turn in the opposite direction has been prescribed for an IFR procedure.
Operating at an aviation event.
Unless otherwise instructed:
Pilots are to maintain two-way radio communication with ATC.
Obtain a clearance prior to taxiing onto the manoeuvring area and prior to takeoff and landing.
Obtain a clearance prior to entering a Control Zone.
If the aircraft is radio equipped, the pilot shall maintain two-way radio communication with FS and advise FS of intention prior to:
Taxiing onto the manoeuvring area.
Prior to takeoff or landing at the aerodrome.
Prior to entering the aerodrome traffic circuit.
If not, radio equipped the pilot must advise FS of intentions by phone.
At aerodromes where runways are defined and promulgated on the aerodrome chart, takeoffs and landings are restricted to those defined runways.
At aerodromes where runways are not promulgated, unless other procedures have been prescribed, aircraft are to:
Land and takeoff into wind, unless good aviation practice in relation to aircraft performance and safety otherwise requires.
Land to the right of any aircraft already landing or taking off.
Takeoff to the right of any aircraft already taking off.
Leave reasonable space to the right for any other aircraft to land or takeoff.
After landing turn left, to observe other traffic and then move clear as soon as practicable.
Move on the ground in line with the direction of landing, and if crossing the runway make all turns left hand and give way to aircraft landing and taking off.
Definitions
Aerodrome Traffic:
All traffic in the manoeuvring area of an aerodrome and all aircraft flying in the vicinity of an aerodrome.
Aerodrome Traffic Circuit:
The pattern flown by aircraft operating in the vicinity of an aerodrome.
Unless otherwise stated or authorised by ATC the standard circuit direction is left hand.
The left-hand circuit gives the pilot the best view of the runway.
There are two ways in which an aircraft can join the circuit:
Joining directly into the circuit.
The aircraft is descended to circuit height prior to joining and makes a straight-in approach (joining on final) or joining downwind or on base.
Carrying out a standard circuit joining procedure.
The standard overhead joining procedure is generally used at unattended aerodromes.
Use the following procedure:
If radio equipped advise traffic of joining intentions.
Approach the aerodrome at 500ft above circuit height.
Pass overhead the aerodrome in order to observe the wind, circuit traffic and any ground signals displayed.
Make all turns in the direction of the traffic circuit.
Once the conditions are ascertained, cross to the non-traffic side, and descend to circuit height.
Turn ninety degrees across wind and pass sufficiently close to the upwind end of the runway to ensure that aircraft taking off can pass safely underneath.
Turn to join the downwind leg of the traffic circuit at a point which ensures adequate spacing with other traffic.
An aviation event is an airshow or similar happening.
If the aviation event has:
Not more than 500 people in attendance, or
Not more than three aircraft participating.
then the Director’s approval is not required.
If there are more than three aircraft, there is no requirement for prior approval if the aircraft are in one formation.
If there are more than 500 people or there are more than three aircraft participating, the organiser must be the holder of an aviation event authorisation issued by the Director.
The PIC of an aircraft taking place in an aviation event shall:
Operate at a height of at least 100ft AGL whilst flying the display except in the case of an agricultural or helicopter display.
Fly sufficiently distanced from spectators, not between the display line and spectators, and not initiating a manoeuvre in the direction of the spectator area.
Not carry passengers.
Each pilot of an aircraft:
Shall, when weather conditions permit, regardless whether the flight is performed under IFR or VFR, maintain a visual lookout so as to see and avoid other aircraft.
That has the right of way, shall maintain heading and speed, but shall not be relieved from the responsibility of taking such action, including collision-avoidance manoeuvres.

Aircraft that are required to give way shall avoid passing over, under, or in front of the other aircraft, unless passing well clear of the aircraft, taking into account the effect of wake turbulence.
When two aircraft approach head on, or approximately so, and there is a danger of collision, each aircraft shall alter heading to the right.
When two aircraft are converging at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft which has the other on its right shall give way except:
Power driven aircraft shall give way to airships, gliders and balloons or aircraft towing anything.
Airships give way to gliders and balloons.
Gliders give way to balloons.
All aircraft give way to parachutes.
An aircraft that is being overtaken has right of way.

The pilot of an aircraft that is overtaking another aircraft shall, if the turn is required to avoid that aircraft, alter heading to the right until it is entirely past and clear of the other aircraft.
Aircraft in flight or on the ground are to give way to aircraft landing or about to land.
When two or more aircraft are approaching for a landing, the higher aircraft is to give way to the lower aircraft, but this rule shall not be used by an aircraft to cut in front of another.
Powered aircraft landing are to give way to gliders landing.
An aircraft that is aware another aircraft is compelled to land shall give way to that aircraft.
Aircraft are not to takeoff until there is no apparent risk of collision with other aircraft.
Aircraft taxiing are to give way to aircraft landing or taking off.
When two aircraft are approaching head on, or nearly so, both aircraft shall stop, or where practicable, alter course to the right so as to remain clear of one another.
When two aircraft are converging, the pilot who has the other to his right shall give way.
When overtaking aircraft, give way and keep well clear of the aircraft being overtaken.
No pilot shall operate an aircraft:
So close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.
In formation flight except by prior arrangement of the PIC of each aircraft.
Other than an aircraft performing a parachute drop operation, in formation flight while carrying passengers for hire or reward.
In an MBZ:
Activates, if equipped, the aircraft’s landing lights or anti-collision lights.
At night:
Position lights; and (3) an anti-collision light system.
A person must not park or move an aircraft at night on a manoeuvring area of an aerodrome that is in use for aircraft operations unless the aircraft:
Is clearly illuminated; or
Has lighted position lights; or
Is in an area that is marked by obstruction lights.

Notwithstanding paragraph (a)(3), a pilot of an aircraft is not required to operate the anti-collision light system if the pilot determines that, because of operating conditions, it is in the best interest of safety to turn the system off.
No person shall enter or remain in any security area or security enhanced area of any designated aerodrome or designated installation, unless that person:
Wears an airport identity card on the front of his or her outer garment; or
Has in his or her possession another identity document or other identity document.
At airports where security measures are in force:
Persons must display identity cards when entering security areas; or
Carry their pilot licence.
No person shall interfere with:
A crew member performing the crew members duties aboard an aircraft; or
Tamper or interfere with any aircraft or its components or fixed or mobile equipment used for the operation or navigation of any aircraft.
No smoking
Every person commits an offence who smokes:
when instructed not to smoke by a crew member, passenger information signs, or placards; or
(b) while on any aircraft that is carrying passengers for hire or reward on any internal flight.

No crew member while acting in his or her official capacity shall be in a state of intoxication or in a state of health in which his or her capacity so to act would be impaired by reason of his or her having consumed or used any intoxicant, sedative, narcotic, or stimulant drug or preparation.

No person may operate, nor may any Operator or Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft allow the operation of, any cellphone or other portable electronic device that is designed to transmit electromagnetic energy, on any aircraft while that aircraft is operating under IFR,
unless the electronic device is one of the following:
(1) hearing aids;
(2) heart pacemakers;
(3) portable voice recorders;
(4) electric shavers;
(5) electronic watches; or

(6) any other portable electronic device if the Operator of the aircraft has determined that the portable electronic device to be operated will not cause interference with any aircraft system or equipment in the aircraft on which it is operated.
Carriage
Carriage by Police
Discharge

During takeoff and landing, passenger baggage shall be stowed in a baggage locker or under the passenger seat provided it does not slide forward under crash impact or hinder evacuation in an emergency.
CAR Part 91.213 requires that during take-off and landing, baggage is stowed in either a baggage locker or under a passenger seat.
This requirement does not apply to balloon operations.
Part 91.215 requires cargo must be carried on a seat, in a cargo rack or bin, or in a cargo compartment. It must also be properly stowed to prevent movement in flight.
Cargo must not exceed load limitations of the seat or floor.

Passengers who appear to be under the influence of alcohol or drugs or exhibit behavioral characteristics which are likely to endanger the aircraft, shall be refused embarkation or, where appropriate removed from the aircraft.
This rule does not apply to search and rescue, or ambulance flights provided reasonable steps have been taken to ensure the safety of the aircraft and passengers.
Disabled passengers shall be appropriately cared for and seated in a position which facilitates evacuation in an emergency.
Escorted passengers can be carried if they do not constitute a safety hazard and prior arrangement has been made with the Operator.
The PIC must be notified whenever disabled or escorted passengers are to be carried.
A pilot must not operate an aircraft:
so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard; or
(2) in formation flight except by prior arrangement with the Pilot-in-Command of each aircraft in the formation.

A pilot of an aircraft shall not allow any object to be dropped from that aircraft in flight unless the pilot has taken reasonable precautions to ensure the dropping of the object does not endanger persons or property.
In classes C,D and G airspace, a speed restriction of 250 kt IAS max applies for flight below 10000ft unless:
The Flight Manual of the aircraft stipulates a minimum safe speed above 250kts, in which case the aircraft must be flown at the minimum safe speed.
The aircraft is being operated at an aviation event.
If flying at Mach .92 or higher you must have approval from the Director.
Passengers, other than persons required to be carried, are not to be carried when it is the intention of the PIC to carry out:
Low flying.
Practice forced landings when flown to below 500ft in a low flying area.
A flight check following maintenance.
Aerobatic flight unless the PIC holds an aerobatic rating.
Display flying at an aviation event.
Any other type of flying specified by the Director.
You shall not fly your aircraft:
At a height not less than that required to execute an emergency landing, without hazard to persons or property on the surface, in the event of an engine failure.

Over any congested area of a city, town or settlement, or over any open-air assembly of people, at a height of less than 1000ft above the highest obstacle in the area within a 600m radius of the aircraft.
Over all other areas, not lower than a height of 500ft above the surface or above a structure or obstacle within a 150m radius.
Fly over congested areas sufficiently high to be able to make a Safe Forced Landing and not lower than 1000ft within 600m of the highest obstacle within the area.
Fly over any other areas not lower than 500ft within 150m of the highest obstacle within the area.
Replace picture
The requirements stated above do not apply when you are conducting one of the following:
A takeoff or landing.
A baulked landing or discontinued approach.
When the PIC is the holder of an Instructor rating and who is conducting flight training or practice flights consisting of:
Simulated engine failures after takeoff commencing below 1000ft above the surface.
Simulated engine failures commencing above 1000ft above the surface, providing the descent below 500ft is conducted within a low flying area.
Flight involving IFR training.
Flights in approved low flying areas.
Flights operating at an approved aviation event.
Flight where the bona fide purpose requires the aircraft to be flown at a lower height (e.g., life raft dropping) provided:
The flight is conducted without hazard to persons or property on the ground.
The aircraft remains outside a horizontal radius of 150m of any person, vessel or structure not associated with the operation.
Only essential persons are carried.
No Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft shall perform a take-off under VFR in an aircraft that has snow, ice, or frost, adhering to the wings, stabilisers, or control surfaces.
No pilot shall operate an aircraft in aerobatic flight:
Over, or within a horizontal distance of 2000ft (600m) of, a congested area of a city or town or settlement.
Over, or within a horizontal distance of 2000ft (600m) of an open-air assembly of persons.
Within any controlled airspace except with the authorisation of ATC.
A pilot may operate an aircraft in aerobatic flight:
Above a height of 3000ft.
Between a height of 1500ft and 3000ft if the pilot holds an aerobatic rating.
Below a height of 1500ft if the pilot holds an aerobatic rating which authorises aerobatic flight to a specified height below 1500ft and is participating in an aviation event.
Each pilot performing a parachute drop operation shall hold a parachute drop rating.
Each pilot performing parachute drop operation shall ensure that:
The aircraft has a valid standard Airworthiness Certificate.
The configuration of the aircraft is appropriate for the operation.
The aircraft has satisfactory room for egress.
The aircraft has no handles or fittings which could cause inadvertent opening of a parachute inside the aircraft.
Suitable points on the aircraft are used to attach static lines.
The aircraft Flight Manual authorises flight with the door removed or open in flight.

Persons on board, not engaged in parachuting operations, occupy seats, are restrained by seat or safety belts, wear and know how to use an approved parachute and have been briefed on emergency procedures.
The parachutists have briefed the PIC on their intended descent.
Each parachutist is authorised by the holder of an Aviation Recreation Organisation certificate or the Director.
No person shall tow a glider or gliders in flight unless that person holds a glider tow rating.
No person shall tow a glider or gliders in flight unless:
The airspeed of the tow aircraft remains below the maximum airspeed specified for the aero-tow in the gliders Flight Manual.
The towing load does not exceed the maximum load specified in the tow Aircraft’s Flight Manual.
The tow hook and tow lines meet approved standards, and the hook is checked for operation prior to flight.
Takeoff, glider release and emergency signals are in conformity with approved procedures.

The takeoff distance to clear a 50ft obstacle with glider(s) in tow does not exceed 85% of the takeoff distance available, and the aircraft can maintain a rate of climb of at least 200ft/min at 1000ft above aerodrome level.
No person shall tow an object other than a glider in flight unless:
They hold a PPL and Tow rating; or
They hold a CPL; or
They hold an ATPL.
The aircraft is equipped with a tow hook with a quick release.
The aircraft has a positive rate of climb at the altitudes to be operated.
No passengers to be carried.
An aircraft operating under Visual Flight Rules must maintain the meteorological minima laid down in the rules.
The fundamental basis of VFR is to see and avoid other aircraft.
VMC means meteorological conditions expressed in terms of visibility, distance from cloud, and ceiling equal to or better than the specified minima.
VMC varies according to the different airspace and type of operation.
If you are flying under VFR, you must maintain VMC.
Conditions less than VMC are called Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC) and you must operate under Instrument Flight Rules (IFR).
Aircraft operating VFR must maintain at least the following Meteorological Minima:

VFR operations may take place in a Control Zone under the prescribed met minima if it is done:
in compliance with an ATC clearance and ATC instructions.
by day only.
clear of clouds.
with a ceiling of at least 600ft.
with a visibility of 1500m.
with the aircraft radio equipped.
When weather conditions at an aerodrome fall below specified meteorological minima, aircraft shall not takeoff or land at that aerodrome.
The aerodrome meteorological minima are:
Controlled Aerodromes / Day and Night:
Minimum ceiling 1500ft.
Minimum visibility 5km.
Uncontrolled Aerodromes:
(for operations under Part 91)

Minimum ceiling 600ft.
Minimum visibility 1500m.
