Minimum ceiling 1500ft.
Minimum visibility 8km.
Frequent mention is made of:
Technical Instructions are instructions for the safe transport of Dangerous Goods by air approved and published by decision of the Council of ICAO.
UN number means a 4-digit number assigned by the United Nations Committee of experts on the transport of Dangerous Goods to identify a substance, or a particular group of substances.
No person shall offer, or accept Dangerous Goods for carriage by air unless the goods are correctly classified, documented, certificated, packaged, marked and labelled.
These goods shall be accepted, handled and carried in accordance with Technical Instructions.
No Forbidden Dangerous Goods shall be offered or accepted for carriage by air unless approved by the Director.
Carriage by police:
Exceptions to the rules which forbid the carriage of Forbidden Dangerous Goods are:
Carriage of Dangerous Goods by the Police provided:
- the aircraft is being operated solely for Police purposes;
- approval has been obtained from the Chief Inspector;
- safety and emergency procedures have been established;
- the goods are in a proper condition for carriage and stowed securely;
- only essential persons are carried on the aircraft, i.e., no passengers;
- the flight is conducted clear of congested areas, city, town, or settlement.
Carriage of goods that are for the recreational use of passengers provided:
- the goods are carried in an unpressurised aircraft of maximum certificated weight of 5700kg or less;
- the flight is a domestic VFR operation and carries only passengers who are associated with the Dangerous Goods;
- the goods are not forbidden under the Technical Instructions for carriage by air in an aircraft that carries passengers;
- safety and emergency procedures have been established.
each item is identified, and the PIC is informed of the dangerous nature of the items;
- the goods are in a proper condition for carriage by air, segregated if required, and properly stowed, secured and packed.

lessons.title: Carriage by Passengers or Crew Members

content.content: Dangerous Goods shall not be carried, or caused to be carried aboard an aircraft by passengers or crew members in carry-on baggage or on their person unless permitted by the Technical Instructions.
Packaging, labelling and marking of Dangerous Goods to be carried by air shall be subject to conditions laid down in the Technical Instructions or by the Director.
Packages shall be marked and labelled showing:
the proper shipping name of the Dangerous Goods and, if applicable, the Technical Name;
when assigned, the corresponding UN number preceded by the letters UN;
the name and address of the person offering the goods, and the consignee (the recipient);
the nature of the hazard prominently written in English on the label; and
any other markings as specified in the Technical Instructions.

Any non-Dangerous Goods offered for carriage by air shall be accompanied by a signed document from the person offering the goods, identifying the nature of the article and certifying that the item is not a Dangerous Goods article.
Exceptions to this requirement are postal articles (i.e. NZ Post does not have to identify each and every article), and 'checked' or carry-on baggage.
Any person offering Dangerous Goods for carriage by air shall ensure that the goods are:
Not forbidden under, and comply with, the Technical Instructions.
Packaged, packed and marked according to the instructions in Subpart B.
Accompanied, when required by the technical instructions, by two copies of a Dangerous Goods transport document.

The main points are that such goods must not be carried in the passenger cabin or flight deck unless the goods are carried as personal goods and approved to be so carried by the Technical Instructions.
DGs labelled “Cargo Aircraft Only” shall only be loaded on cargo aircraft.
If damage or leakage is discovered when unloading Dangerous Goods, the Operator shall inspect the area concerned and remove any hazardous contamination.
If infectious substances appear to be damaged or leaking, the Operator shall:
avoid handling the package(s) or keep the handling to a minimum;
inspect adjacent packages for contamination and put aside any that have been contaminated;
inform the appropriate health or veterinary authority and provide information on countries of transit where any person may have been exposed to danger; and
notify the consignor (sender) or consignee (recipient).

If contamination by radioactive materials has been shown, the aircraft shall be taken out of service immediately, and not returned to service until contamination has been reduced to levels which do not exceed the values specified in the Technical Instructions.
The Operator shall present the PIC with a dedicated form stating the nature of Dangerous Goods carried in the aircraft.
Also, the PIC shall be provided with information, readily available during flight, for use in an emergency response to accidents or incidents involving the Dangerous Goods being carried.

lessons.title:
Information to Passengers 
and in Cargo Acceptance Areas

content.content: Each Operator shall display sufficient numbers of public notices, prominently located at cargo acceptance areas, providing information about the carriage of Dangerous Goods.
Each Operator shall inform passengers of the type of goods that they are prohibited from carrying aboard the aircraft.
Before commencing a flight, the PIC must obtain and become familiar with all information concerning that flight including:
The current Meteorological information.
The fuel requirements.
The alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed.
Any known or likely traffic delays that have been notified by ATS.
The status of the communication and navigation facilities to be used.
The current conditions of the aerodrome and runway lengths of runways at aerodromes of intended use.
Any takeoff and landing distance data contained in the aircraft Flight Manual.
In the case of a multi-engine aircraft:
- Engine inoperative procedures.
- One engine inoperative performance data.
Before commencing a flight, the pilot of the aircraft shall be familiar with:
The aircraft’s Flight Manual.
Any placards, listings, instrument markings, or combination of these, containing any operating limitation prescribed for that aircraft by the manufacturer or the Director.
The emergency equipment installed on the aircraft.
Which crew member is assigned to operate the emergency equipment.
The procedures to be followed for the use of the emergency equipment in an emergency situation.

CAR Part 91 stipulates that the PIC shall not begin a VFR flight unless, in the forecast weather conditions, the aeroplane has sufficient fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing at the planned normal cruising speed and to fly:
During the day, after that for at least 30 minutes. (20 minutes, or equal to the anticipated flight time if less than 20 minutes, for Helicopter operations).
At night, after that for at least 45 minutes.
Under Part 91 fuelling with Class 3.1C & D
the engines can be running, but still no passengers.
No aircraft should be refuelled or defuelled where there is undue risk for any third party.

In the case of fuel spillage on an impermeable surface, fuelling must cease, and immediate action taken to cover the fuel with sand, sawdust, foam or similar materials, and the aircraft moved away from the contaminated area before an engine is started.
A flight plan achieves two important objectives.
It is a method of providing ATS with the intended route.
It provides a flight following service, whereby the appropriate authorities will be notified if the aircraft becomes overdue.
Flight plans can be lodged with the National Briefing Office by internet, fax or by phone.
A flight plan shall be filed for the following flights operating under
Part 91:
For flights more than 50 miles from shore.
The PIC requires an alerting service.
A flight plan may be filed for any other flight conducted under VFR.
An alerting service is the notification by an ATS unit to appropriate organisations of the requirement for search and rescue of aircraft and assisting the organisations as required.
All ATS units provide an alerting service to all flights on a flight plan and, as far as practicable, to all flights known to ATS.

lessons.title: Content of a VFR Flight Plan

content.content: A VFR flight plan must include the following information:
The aircraft registration and callsign.
The aircraft type.
The route, including where practicable for each route segment, aerodromes of departure and intended landing, estimated elapsed times, and time on the ground at each intermediate aerodrome.
The SARTIME.
Total fuel endurance.
The total number of persons in the aircraft.
The name and telephone contact details of the PIC.
The name of the aircraft owner or Operator.
Any additional information that will assist SAR.
Where a VFR flight plan has been submitted the PIC must:
Inform an appropriate ATS unit of any change to the details in the flight plan and of any change to the SARTIME before the expiry of that SARTIME.
Terminate the flight plan by advising an appropriate unit before the SARTIME.
ETA is the estimated time of arrival at the aerodrome where as SARTIME is the time at which (if exceeded) search and rescue will start searching for the overdue aircraft.
Search and rescue will be initiated immediately if SARTIME is breached. The details can be found in AIPNZ General section.
UNICOM (Universal Communications) is not an air traffic service.
UNICOM is an air/ground communications facility providing an information service at aerodromes with no aerodrome control or aerodrome flight information service.
Information provided may include:
- Current aerodrome information and conditions;
- Basic weather information such as:
- Wind direction and strength
- Visibility
- Cloud cover
- Temperature
- QNH
- Meteorological reports
- Aerodrome and Weather Information Broadcasts (AWIB).
The UNICOM Operator may also provide other ancillary services.
AFRU (Aerodrome Frequency Response Unit)
An AFRU is a unit that provides confirmation to pilots that they have selected the correct aerodrome frequency, and that their aircraft radio is operating correctly.
It may operate as a supplementary device to a ground facility (UNICOM) operating on the aerodrome frequency, or it may be the sole ground communications device.
AWIB (Aerodrome and Weather Information Broadcasts)

An AWIB is an automated broadcast on a specified frequency at some unattended aerodromes. It relays information on meteorological and operational conditions that are obtained from automatic sensors and manual observations.
An AWIB is not provided by an air traffic service and is therefore not required to have the same standard of accuracy as an ATIS does.
Each Pilot-in-Command of an aircraft on a VFR flight shall, when operating in controlled airspace, report the position of the aircraft to ATC at the times or reporting points required by ATC.
(2) obtain an ATC clearance from that service before:
(i) taxiing on any portion of the manoeuvring area; or
(ii) landing at or taking-off from any runway or heliport at that aerodrome; or
(iii) entering a control zone.
Content of a VFR Position report:
Visual position reports should contain those elements of the following that are applicable to the reason for the report:
identification;
SSR code (if on discrete code);
position;
time;
altitude;
intended route;
next reporting point; and
ETA at next reporting point.

lessons.title: Compliance with ATC Clearances and Instructions

content.content: A pilot shall:
Comply with any ATC clearance or instruction.
When a deviation from an ATC clearance or instruction is required for the safe operation of the aircraft, notify ATC of that deviation as soon as possible.
A pilot shall not comply with an ATC clearance or instruction if such compliance is a violation of any rule.

An aerodrome flight information service is the provision of information and advice useful for the safe and efficient conduct of flights within the vicinity of aerodromes that have a Flight Service Station (FSS).
A small number of aerodromes have a FSS providing an Aerodrome Flight Information Service (AFIS).
AFIS does not issue clearances or instructions.
All ATS units provide a flight information service to varying degrees.
Flight information includes the following:
Traffic information relating to other known aircraft in your vicinity.
NOTAM information.
Some Meteorological information.
Other significant information relating to your flight.
On request, advice relating to questions you may have regarding your flight.
The main provider of a flight information service for New Zealand is Christchurch Information.
Christchurch information provides information for the whole country.
They do not provide a control service; they do not separate aircraft.
You may contact Christchurch Information during any flight, whether you have filed a flight plan or not.
You must have a clearance to fly in any controlled airspace.
You must have the clearance before you enter controlled airspace, so it is better to request it 5 to 10 minutes prior.
Remember to read back the clearance.
The specific direction from one aircraft to another is usually expressed using the 12-hour clock method.
12 o'clock means directly ahead,
3 o'clock means directly to the right,
6 o'clock means directly behind,
and 9 o'clock means directly to the left.
Difference between Class C and D airspace?
No separation in Class G,
only information.
The Pilot-in-Command is responsible for separation at all times, and most importantly whenever ATC is not responsible for separation.
Visual separation requires that the controller or one or both pilots have the conflicting traffic in sight.
Vertical separation is assured when aircraft fly at levels 1000ft apart when below FL290.

500ft may be used in controlled airspace between an IFR aircraft and a VFR aircraft provided both are medium or light weight category and the lower aircraft is VFR or Special VFR operating at an altitude of 4500ft or below.
Horizontal separation can be achieved by distance or time intervals between aircraft.
It can also be radar separation.
The minimum radar separation distance between two aircraft at similar levels is 5nm.

Radar Control, radar advisory and radar information services, as appropriate, are provided to VFR flights under area radar or approach radar control within radar coverage in Class C and Class D airspace.
Radar services are not normally provided to VFR flights within radar coverage operating in Class G airspace.
Every effort will be made to provide a service if requested, but it will be limited to:
assisting aircraft experiencing an emergency; or
giving navigational assistance; or
aircraft crossing Cook Strait.

Some control towers provide Area and Approach Control services in controlled airspace but most of the control of aircraft in controlled airspace is provided by radar controllers in the three Control Centres in NZ, situated at:
Auckland,
Wellington and
Christchurch.
There are two types of radar used in NZ:
Primary Surveillance Radar (PSR), and
Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR).
Primary radar works by sending out a signal and receiving a ‘reflection’ back from the aircraft.
The advantage of primary radar is that the aircraft does not require any extra equipment.
The disadvantage is that thick clouds, flocks of birds etc. can interfere with the signal.
There are three primary radars in NZ.
Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch.
They each have a range of 80 nm.
Secondary Surveillance radar works by sending a signal out to an aircraft which triggers a signal to be returned by the aircraft’s transponder.
An advantage is that a code (mode A) and the aircraft’s altitude (mode C) can be sent with the return signal.
The disadvantage is that only aircraft fitted with serviceable transponders will be detected by the radar.
The range of SSR is much greater than PSR at approximately 250nm.
There are 6 SSR installations in NZ.
Both PSR and SSR rely on ‘line of sight’ transmission and reception, this means that coverage can be reduced by intervening terrain.
SSRs, with a maximum range of 256 NM, are located at the following sites:
Ruaotuwhenua 12.5 NM north-west of Auckland Airport;
; Te Weraiti Kaimai Range 6.5 NM east of Matamata Township
Ballance Tararua Range between Palmerston North aerodrome and Pahiatua Township;
Hawkins Hill 3.5 NM west of Wellington Airport;
Mt Robertson 3 NM south-east of Picton Township;
Cass Peak Port Hills 9.5 NM south-east of Christchurch Airport.
The national system comprises of nine radar sites.
These sites feed the main Airways computers and information is then passed to the appropriate ATS units.
Radar can provide the following to VFR flights:
Control in class C & D airspace and assistance in class G if there is an emergency.
Navigation Assistance.
Radar Vectoring.
Traffic Information.
Weather information.
If a speed restriction is applied by radar, it should be maintained to within 10kts.
Altitude:
The vertical level, a point, or an object considered as a point, measured from mean sea level.
Height:
The vertical distance of a level, a point or an object considered as a point, measured from a specific datum and includes the vertical dimension of an object.
Thus, altitude is measured from sea level and height is measured from any nominated point, normally ground level (AGL).
The term elevation is often used to indicate the vertical distance of the ground measured from mean sea level.
When flying below 13,000ft, the altimeter subscale is to be set to the appropriate setting.
The following different settings are used:
Aerodrome QNH is the calculated mean sea level pressure at the aerodrome.
With QNH set, the altimeter will indicate altitude (height above mean sea level).
ATC will advise you of the correct aerodrome QNH at uncontrolled aerodromes. QNH can be obtained by setting the airfield elevation.
Aerodrome QNH is used when operating in the control zone.

The pilot of an aircraft departing from an aerodrome where no QNH setting is available must set aerodrome elevation on the altimeter prior to departure and obtain the appropriate altimeter setting from an ATS unit as soon as possible, and in any case, before entering IMC.
Area QNH is the QNH setting applicable whilst flying within a QNH Zone.
NZ is divided into 12 QNH zones from the surface to 13,000ft.
Area QNH is to be used when outside the control zone and will be transmitted by the appropriate ATS unit.
Replaced picture
Aerodrome QFE is the atmospheric pressure at aerodrome elevation.
With QFE set, the altimeter will indicate height above the aerodrome.
When flying above 13,000ft your altitudes are now referred to as Flight Levels.
Flight Levels mean surfaces of constant atmospheric pressure which are related to a specific pressure datum of 1013.2hPa.
As you climb through 13,000ft you change your altimeter setting to 1013.2.
This altitude is known as the Transition Altitude, you are then flying at Flight Levels.
Examples:
When you descend through FL150 you change the subscale setting to zone QNH.
This level is known as the Transition Level.
The Transition Level becomes FL160 when the zone QNH for the area is 980hPa or less; and when within a 20nm radius of Mount Cook for aircraft in IMC.
The layer between the Transition Altitude and Transition Level is known as the Transition Layer.
You are not allowed to cruise in the Transition Layer without ATS clearance in controlled airspace.

In uncontrolled airspace you can only cruise in the Transition Layer if you are unable to operate outside that range, and you have established there will be no conflict with other aircraft, and you have advised ATS of your intentions.
A PIC may not fly level:
In the Transition Layer unless authorised by ATC.
At any Flight Level below FL160 when an area QNH is 980hPa or less.

The domestic VFR magnetic track rules require that VFR flights, other than gliders, operating in level cruising flight above 3000 ft AMSL or 1000ft above the ground (whichever is higher) must be flown at an altitude or Flight Level appropriate to the magnetic tracks as specified in the VFR table of cruising levels.
These cruising levels are:
When flying at or below 13000 ft AMSL:
For a Northerly Magnetic track (270°M through North to 089°M)
Fly odd thousands plus 500ft.

Fly even thousands plus 500ft.
When flying level at or above FL150 up to and including FL275:
For a Northerly Magnetic track (270°M through North to 089°M)
Fly odd flight levels plus 500ft beginning at and including FL155.
For a Southerly Magnetic track (090°M through South to 269°M)
Fly even flight levels plus 500ft beginning at and including FL165.

VFR Flights 4.2.2, CAR 91.313 requires the pilot of an aircraft, other than a glider or hang glider, operating under VFR in level cruising flight at more than 3000ft AMSL or 1000ft AGL (whichever is the higher) to fly at an altitude or FL appropriate to the track as specified in Table ENR 1.7-2: New Zealand FIR Table of Cruising Levels.
The exceptions to this are:
when otherwise authorised by ATC during flight within, entering or leaving Class C and D airspace; or
when operating within controlled airspace, where ATC may assign IFR levels to VFR aircraft.
ATC will assign these altitudes with the phrase ‘NON-Standard VFR’ following the cleared altitude.
A PIC of an aircraft operating in transponder mandatory (TM) airspace unless otherwise authorised or instructed by ATC:
Operate the transponder, including Mode C.
Set the code assigned by ATC or appropriate general code.
In the event of an in-flight emergency, loss of radio communication or an act of unlawful interference set the appropriate code.
ATC permission must be obtained prior to operating in transponder mandatory airspace when:
The transponder only has Mode A capability, or it is not working.
The aircraft is not equipped with a transponder, in this case permission must be requested at least 30 minutes prior to departure of the flight.
On maps and charts, airspace that requires a transponder is indicated by the letters TM (Transponder Mandatory).
D
TM
Transponders are not required in Class G airspace.
The following codes are permanently allocated and, except when instructed by ATC, the appropriate code should be selected on the transponder in the following situations:
VFR – fixed wing aircraft 1200
VFR – helicopters 1500
VFR – gliders and balloons 1300
VFR – powered aircraft in GAAs 1400 NZAIP Vol 1 & 4
Any aircraft subjected to unlawful interference (hijacking)
Any aircraft suffering a radio failure
Any aircraft in an emergency situation
Controllers may allocate a discrete code to individual aircraft so that each aircraft with a discrete code is more easily identified and tracked on the radar screen.
Whenever an aircraft squawks 7500, 7600 or 7700 an alarm system notifies the radar controller, therefore you should always place the transponder on STBY when changing codes.
Transponders must be tested and inspected every 24 calendar months.
Transponder testing should be done in shielded areas with adherence to the following:
Notify the nearest ATC unit giving the time of testing.
Use transponder codes between 0050 and 0057.
If testing mode C, set to 40,000ft or above if possible.
Class A: (Controlled)
A clearance is required.
All flights are separated.
No VFR flights allowed.
Class B: (Controlled)
A clearance is required.
All flights are separated.
Classes A & B only apply in International Airspace.
Class C: (Controlled)
A clearance is required.
VFR flights are separated from IFR flights day and night.
Special VFR flights are separated from IFR flights.
Special VFR flights are separated from other Special VFR flights when visibility is less than 5km.
VFR flights are not separated from other VFR flights day and night.
VFR flights are provided with traffic information about other VFR flights, considering ATC or FIS service priorities.
NOTE: Traffic information and avoidance falls short of full ATC separation, but it does assist pilots in providing their own separation from other aircraft.
Class D: (Controlled)
A clearance is required.
VFR flights are not separated from IFR flights.
VFR flights are separated from other Special VFR flights when visibility is less than 5km.
IFR flights are provided with traffic information about VFR flights during daylight hours.
VFR flights are provided with traffic information about all flights as far as practical.
Class E: (Controlled)
This airspace has been made obsolete in NZ
Class F: (Uncontrolled)
Not currently used in NZ
Class G: (Uncontrolled)
A clearance is not required.
There is no separation provided.
IFR flights receive traffic information about other IFR flights, and VFR may receive information on request.
A Flight Information Region is an airspace of defined dimensions within which Flight Information and Alerting Services are provided.
It extends from ground or sea level to an unlimited upper level, encompassing all other types of airspace.
The world is divided into FIRs, and NZ is within the Auckland Oceanic FIR (NZZO).
Within the Auckland Oceanic FIR is the NZ Domestic FIR (NZZC) served by the Christchurch Flight Information Centre.
Within the NZ FIR there are two types of controlled airspace:
Control Zones (CTR) and Control Areas (CTA).
An Air Traffic Control service is the provision of Control in order to prevent collisions and the maintenance of an orderly flow of traffic.
Air Traffic Control includes:
Area Control Service.
Approach Control Service.
Aerodrome Control Service.
Aircraft are required to be radio equipped in controlled airspace.
Special arrangements can be made with ATC for NORDO (No-Radio) to operate in controlled airspace.
A radio is not required to fly in Class G airspace.
A CTR is controlled airspace of defined dimensions surrounding one or more aerodromes extending upwards from the surface to a specified upper limit within which only authorised flights are permitted.
A clearance is required to fly in a CTR.
CTRs can be class C or D and are all Transponder Mandatory.
AIP ENR 5.1
CTRs can be any shape to best suit the traffic
and they always start from ground or sea level – therefore you cannot fly underneath a CTR.
A CTA is controlled airspace of defined dimensions that extends from a specified lower limit to a specified upper limit.
A CTA is generally established to encompass IFR routes.
A clearance is required to fly in a CTA.
Entered new slide
Where different classes of airspace adjoin one above the other, at the common level, a pilot may comply with the requirements of the less restrictive class of airspace.
VFR Transit Lanes are areas of uncontrolled airspace established in controlled airspace.
They are active during daylight hours only.
VFR aircraft do not need a clearance to fly in a VFR transit lane.
VFR Transit Lanes are shown on VNCs by solid blue lines.
The letter “T” followed by a 3-digit figure and a name identifies the airspace, e.g., T187 RONDA.
VFR training and glider areas have been established as General Aviation Areas (GAAs) to facilitate VFR training and glider flying in CTR or CTA airspace clear of IFR traffic.
These areas are only available during daylight hours.
When in a GAA you must maintain a continuous listening watch on the appropriate frequency.
There are three types of GAA:
Active during daylight hours
VFR aircraft may use the GAA without reference to ATC.
Active when notified to ATC
Pilots of VFR aircraft must notify ATC prior to entry and prior to exit.
Active when approved by ATC
VFR pilots must obtain ATC approval for the activation of the GAA.
GAAs are designated by NZG, abbreviated to G---
Each PIC shall on a VFR flight, when operating in controlled airspace, report the position of the aircraft to ATC at the times or reporting points required by ATC.

There is no legal requirement to make regular position reports outside controlled airspace and when on cross-country flights, however good airmanship and safety dictate that regular position reporting is desirable.
A Visual Reporting Point (VRP) is a promulgated point usually a town or landmark on a Visual Navigation Chart (VNC) or an AIP chart. Pilots should make position reports in reference to the VRPs.
When CTA and CTR are not operative, the rules and procedures for Class G airspace apply.

Hours of service of all ATS units are published by SUP and may also be amended by NOTAM. Since there is a possibility of change to ATS hours of service, pilots intending to operate within CTA or CTR outside the promulgated hours of service should, prior to entry, confirm with the unit’s ATIS or the Christchurch ATSC that the service is not operating.
Restricted Areas are established within NZ in the public interest or for safety reasons.
The public interest includes areas protected for conservation purposes, and special events.
Safety reasons include areas prescribed for police or search and rescue operations.
Aircraft are not prohibited from operating within a Restricted Area, but may only enter an active Restricted Area with the prior approval of the designated controlling authority.
Restricted Areas are depicted on charts with the designation R---
Military Operational areas are established to encompass intensive military operations, including live firing.
A clearance from the controlling authority must be received prior to entry.
Military Operational areas are depicted with the designation M---
Mandatory Broadcast zones are established to provide increased protection to aircraft in areas of uncontrolled airspace where high density or special operations may occur.
An MBZ requires a pilot to transmit position and intention reports on a specified frequency at entry, exit and at least every 10 minutes while operating within an MBZ.
Landing lights and anti-collision lights are to be used.
Mandatory Broadcast Zones are depicted with the designation B---
Non-radio equipped (NORDO) aircraft must not enter an MBZ unless they have another station, such as an ATS unit or an aircraft, broadcasting the required reports on their behalf.
Volcanic Hazard Zones are established to increase protection to aircraft in an area where volcanic activity may be present.
Operation in a VHZ requires pilots to operate in VMC by day.
Volcanic Hazard Zones are depicted with the designation V---
Danger Areas are established to warn pilots of an area where danger to aviation may be present.
A Danger Area requires pilots to have due consideration of the danger present within the area but does not require approval from any agency.
Danger Areas are depicted on charts with the designation D---
Low Flying Zones are established to facilitate pilot training in low level techniques.
A Low Flying Zone extends from the surface to 500ft.
No pilot shall operate an aircraft within a Low Flying Zone unless that pilot:
Is receiving dual flight instruction.
Is authorised and briefed on the boundaries of the area and the method of entry and exit from the area by an Instructor.
Complies with the conditions of operation in the LFZ.
Prior to entering the area, broadcasts, on the appropriate frequency, details of the flight and the proposed elapsed time in the area.
Maintains a listening watch on the appropriate frequency while in the area and broadcasts when exiting.
Dual low flying may be conducted with a visibility of not less than 1500m.
No passengers are carried.
Low Flying Zones are designated by NZL---
VFR Common Frequency Zones fulfill a similar function in uncontrolled airspace as the MBZ around uncontrolled aerodromes.
The procedures described are not mandatory, but it is good airmanship to comply with those requirements.
Feilding CFZ
The Director may, in the interests of aviation safety or security, or for any other reason in the public interest, designate an area as a Temporary Control Area or Temporary Control Zone.
These temporary airspaces should not exceed a period of three months.
It is important to remain aware of changes to airspace. Charts are frequently updated, and a list of current airspace can be found in the AIP ENR section and the CAA website.
One recent change is the discontinuation of Parachute Drop Zones. These are now Parachute Landing Areas (PLA) and should be treated as Danger Areas.
Aerodrome:

Any defined area of land or water intended or designed to be used either wholly or partly for landing, departure, and surface movement of aircraft; and includes any buildings, installations and equipment on or adjacent to any such area used in conjunction with the aerodrome or its administration.
Runway:
A defined rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for the landing and taking off for aircraft.
Runway Strip:
A defined area symmetrically including the runway.
Taxiway:
A defined path on a land aerodrome established for the taxiing of aircraft and intended to provide a link between one part of the aerodrome and another.
Apron:
A defined area on a land aerodrome intended to accommodate aircraft for the purpose of loading or unloading passengers or cargo, refuelling, parking or maintenance.
Manoeuvring Area:

That part of the aerodrome used for takeoff and landing of aircraft and for the surface movement of aircraft associated with takeoff and landing, but does not include areas set aside for loading, unloading or maintenance of aircraft.
Movement Area:
That part of the aerodrome used for takeoff and landing of aircraft and for the surface movement of aircraft and includes the manoeuvring area, maintenance areas and aprons.
Vicinity of an Aerodrome:
An area around an aerodrome, extending laterally not more than 10 nm from the aerodrome, where aircraft carry out manoeuvres associated with entering, leaving, or operating within the circuit.
No person may use any place as an aerodrome unless that place is suitable for the purpose of taking off or landing of the aircraft concerned.

AIPNZ AD 1.4-2 para 3.1 states that aerodromes in New Zealand are divided into two groups:
those that are certificated in accordance with CAR Part 139, and
those that are not certificated.
Many aerodromes are ‘certificated’ which means that they meet minimum standards of design and safety, provide the required level of rescue and fire fighting and comply with many other requirements.
Both privately owned and publicly owned aerodromes can be certificated.
Public aerodromes are available to aircraft that can comply with any operational conditions prescribed for the aerodrome.
Privately owned and operated aerodromes can only be used subject to any conditions specified by the Owner or Operator of the aerodrome.
Generally, the Operator's permission will be required.
Some are ‘available for general use’, which means you do not need prior permission from the Operator before using the aerodrome.
Military aerodromes can only be used by civil aircraft with the permission of the base commander, except for ambulance and mercy flights.

Aerodrome Controllers give clearances, instructions and information to aircraft operating in the vicinity of the aerodrome and on the manoeuvring area, to prevent collisions and to achieve runway and wake turbulence separations.
Aerodrome Controllers usually use visual means.
At some busy aerodromes, radar may be installed.
The following is a list of priorities that can be applied by ATC in the following order:
An aircraft in an emergency situation.
A Multi-Engine aircraft with a failed engine.
An aircraft with radio failure.
An ambulance flight.
An aircraft on SAR missions.
An aircraft carrying the Governor General, PM, or visiting Head-of-State.
Landing aircraft priority over takeoffs.
An aircraft landing or taking off over aircraft taxiing.
An aircraft which is first able to use the manoeuvring area or desired airspace in the normal course of its operation will be given priority.
Controlled Aerodromes:
These are aerodromes with an Air Traffic Control unit providing an aerodrome control service.
Uncontrolled Aerodromes:
These are aerodromes that do not have an Air Traffic Control service. At these aerodromes, pilots are responsible for the separation between themselves and others.
Attended Aerodromes:
Attended Aerodromes that provide either Air Traffic Control or Aerodrome Flight Information Service.
Unattended Aerodromes:
Unattended aerodromes are those that have neither ATC nor AFIS.
The Air Traffic Service and radio frequencies provided at an aerodrome are shown on the aerodrome chart.
‘Tower’ means an Aerodrome Control Service is provided.
‘Flight Service’ means an Aerodrome Flight Information Service is Provided.
‘Unattended’ means that no air traffic service is provided.
The hours that Air Traffic services are provided are listed in the NZAIP and by NOTAM.
Where an ATC or Aerodrome Flight Information Service is provided, pilots must, on all occasions, notify the ATS unit the nature of their intended movement before taxiing onto the manoeuvring area.

For all operations at an aerodrome where an ATS unit is in operation, radio equipped aircraft are required to advise the ATS unit of the number of persons on board the aircraft prior to taxiing onto the manoeuvring area, and also on first contact with the aerodrome ATS unit when arriving at the aerodrome.
Most Controlled Aerodromes have an Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS), this is a recorded message broadcast on an appropriate frequency listed in the Volume 4.
Before taxi and prior to arrival, pilots should listen to the ATIS and on first contact with the Tower, advise that you are in receipt of the ATIS and read back the QNH. e.g.
……. information Charlie One Zero One Three.
Some uncontrolled aerodromes have an Aerodrome and Weather Information Broadcast (AWIB).
This is a recorded message containing weather information such as wind, and runway in use etc.

When flying in the vicinity of a controlled aerodrome, pilots are required to maintain a continuous listening watch on the appropriate frequency or, if this is not possible, watch out for and comply with light signals.
Pilots are to obtain a clearance prior to taxiing on the manoeuvring area, taking off, joining the circuit and landing.

Most aircraft in New Zealand have been given a Group Rating number.
The Group Rating number for the runway represents the highest Group Rating authorised.

Aircraft Incident:
Any incident, not otherwise classified, associated with the operation of an aircraft.
Aerodrome Incident:
An incident involving an aircraft operation and:
An obstruction on an aerodrome.
A defective visual aid.
A defective surface or manoeuvring area.
Any other defective aerodrome facility.
Airspace Incident:
An incident involving deviation from, or shortcomings of, the procedures or rules for:
Avoiding collisions between aircraft.
Avoiding collisions between aircraft and other obstacles when an aircraft is being provided with an Air Traffic Service.
Bird Incident:
There is a collision between an aircraft and one or more birds.
When one or more birds pass sufficiently close to an aircraft in flight to cause alarm to the pilot.
Details:
Means a written report on what happened, being it an accident or an incident.
Describing what happened, who was involved, where the occurrence happened etc.
Fatal Injury:
Any injury that results in death within 30 days of the accident.
Occurrence:
An accident or incident.
Security incident:
An incident that involves unlawful interference.
Serious Incident:
An incident involving circumstances indicating that an accident nearly occurred.
Serious Injury:
Any injury that is sustained by a person in an accident and that:
Requires hospitalisation for more than 48 hours, commencing with seven days from the date the injury was received.
Results in the fracture of any bone, except simple fractures of fingers, toes, or nose.
Involves lacerations which cause severe haemorrhage, nerve, muscle, or tendon damage.
Involves injury to an internal organ.
Involves second- or third-degree burns, or any burns affecting more than 5% of the body surface.
Involves verified exposure to infectious substances or injurious radiation.
TAIC:
Transport Accident Investigation Commission.

Each PIC of an aircraft that is involved in an accident or, if that person is fatally or seriously injured, or if the aircraft is missing, the Operator, shall notify the Authority of the accident as soon as practicable.
The notification shall be in a manner acceptable to the authority.
Details of the accident or incident must be submitted within 10 days of the occurrence.

A summary of an accident which requires notification is an occurrence in which a person is killed or seriously injured, or in which an aircraft suffers damage or structural failure that adversely affects its structural strength, performance or flight characteristics, and that requires major repair or replacement of the component affected.
If death, injury or damage to any third-party property occurs, the PIC is required to advise the NZ Police.
Each PIC of an aircraft that is involved in an Incident, shall notify the Authority of the incident as soon as practicable.
The notification shall be in a manner acceptable to the authority.
Details of the incident must be submitted within 14 days of the occurrence.
Where, in any emergency described in this section, a Pilot-in-Command or an Operator breaches the Act or regulations or rules made under the Act, the Pilot-in-Command or the Operator, shall:
immediately notify the relevant air traffic control service of the action; and

(b) as soon as practicable, notify the Director of the action and the circumstances that necessitated it and, if requested by the Director, provide to the Director a written report in respect of the action.

content.content: No person shall have access to, interfere with, or remove an aircraft or its components involved in an accident unless authorised to do so by the CAA.
The Authority may permit access, interference or removal in order to:
Remove persons or livestock from the aircraft or wreckage.
Protect the aircraft, including its contents, from further damage.
Disconnect or de-activate Cockpit Voice Recorder, flight data recorder, or emergency locator beacon.
Prevent obstruction to the public, or to air navigation, if no practical alternative is available.

Any wreckage, components, mail or cargo removed shall be moved only so far as necessary to ensure its safety, be kept in separate distinct areas to indicate from which part of the aircraft it has been taken and, where possible, have sketches or photographs of the original position of the items.
Each holder of a certificate of registration of an aircraft that is involved in a serious incident or accident shall preserve all records for at least 14 days after the serious incident or accident.

“YES” or “ROGER” activate transmitter once.
(b) “NO” activate transmitter twice.

When it is necessary for a pilot to direct a surface craft to the place where an aircraft or surface craft is in distress, the pilot should do so by transmitting precise instructions by any means available. If such precise instructions cannot be transmitted, they should be given by carrying out the following procedure:
(a) circle the surface craft at least once;
(b) cross the projected course of the surface craft close ahead at low altitude:
(i) rocking the aircraft; or
(ii) opening and closing the throttle; or
(iii) changing the propeller pitch.
(c) then heading in the direction in which the surface craft is to be directed and
(d) repeat these procedures until the surface craft acknowledges.
